key_insight: VLMs often produce 'correct' answers to classic visual illusions by recalling memorized patterns rather than perceiving the visual change—models tend to repeat the same response even when illusion factors are inverted, unlike humans.
problem_solved: Distinguishes whether VLM outputs reflect genuine visual perception or memorized training associations, providing a systematic way to diagnose when models are blind to obvious visual changes.
method: Construct a benchmark of classic visual illusions with controlled manipulations (inversions/counterfactuals) to test perceptual sensitivity.
Probe multiple VLMs with standardized prompts and compare model responses to human judgments, measuring invariance to visual change.
Use targeted ablations and probing analyses (e.g., perturb visual input, isolate encoder vs. decoder contributions, vary prompt context) to separate perception from recall.
impact: Reveals a key failure mode in VLM evaluation and deployment: high-level correctness can mask lack of true perceptual grounding. This guides practitioners to design more robust benchmarks, training regimes, and interpretability checks that prioritize perceptual fidelity over memorized cues.
visual_elements: Side-by-side original vs inverted illusion image with model and human answers annotated to show divergent sensitivity.
Bar chart showing response invariance rates across multiple VLMs (percent unchanged after inversion).
Flow diagram of the probing pipeline: dataset → prompts → model responses → human baseline → ablation analyses.
Heatmap or attention overlay indicating which image regions feed the model's decision (to illustrate reliance on local cues vs global perception).
paper_title: Do VLMs Perceive or Recall? Probing Visual Perception vs. Memory with Classic Visual Illusions
paper_authors: Xiaoxiao Sun, Mingyang Li, Kun yuan, Min Woo Sun, Mark Endo
